newsitem.title: UK: Mark in tug-of-war between German recovery and EMU.
newsitem.headline: Mark in tug-of-war between German recovery and EMU.

text.p: Signs that Germany's economy is on the mend are tempting the currency market to push the mark higher.
But it is shackled by the view that a stronger German economy would boost chances of European economic and monetary union (EMU) going ahead -- traditionally bad news for the mark.
The conflicting views have tended to cancel each other out and left the net impact on the German currency slight.
"The market hasn't developed a clear response to strength in German economic data," said Paul Brunker, European strategist at Robert Fleming.

"It's easy enough to push the mark up against the dollar on the basis of the German data as that's straightforward. But the problem with marking it up against the French franc or lira is that the ramifications are ambiguous," Brunker said.
Some analysts believe relief that Europe's biggest economy has weathered the worst of its economic problems is likely to win out over the EMU issue for now.
This is because the perception of an improving German economy is a more enduring one, while excitement over the launch of Europe's single currency tends to come and go, they said.

"The fact that the economy is going to look better should be supportive...and there is a bit of a whipsawing that goes on in terms of sentiment (over EMU). It tends to swing from optimism to pessimism," said Michael Lewis, senior economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
The latest clash of perceptions came on Thursday, when the mark firmed after data showed Germany's February industrial production had grown more strongly than expected.

It then dipped against other European currencies when Chancellor Helmut Kohl, the most prominent champion of EMU, declared he would run for reelection in 1998 and said EMU would start punctually in 1999 with Germany meeting the necessary conditions.

Recovery in the German economy would mean an improvement in the nation's budget deficit and an easing of worries about Bonn's ability to meet the target of a three percent budget deficit-to-gross domestic product ratio set for participation in EMU.

This in turn leads to optimism about EMU and its timetable. EMU optimism has been seen as negative for the mark because of a perception that the mark will be replaced by a unit which is not as stable or credible.
Kohl's confirmation that he will join the race for Chancellor again caused few jitters in the market.
"It marginally increased the possibility of a prompt start to EMU but not significantly. In any case most pundits seemed to have been believing he would run again," Fleming's Brunker said.
Analysts agreed the currency market seems to have pushed monetary union on to the back burner for now but said the issue was likely to boil up again in the near future.

"EMU sentiment isn't so strong at this moment. But over the next few months it's going to come back into people's minds and we might see some more rumblings out of Germany about who gets in and who doesn't," said Francis Breedon, foreign exchange economist at Lehman Brothers.

"At the moment their (German authorities') focus is very much on themselves and they've been very quiet...because they want to get their own affairs in order before they start talking about anybody else," Breedon said.
In any event, the mark's moves against its European counterparts were likely to be mild, as has been the case in recent months, some analysts said.
